Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent

vLLM CVE-2026-48746 auth bypass via malformed Host header on /v1/* (`/` or `?` in Host) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact exploitation primitive in CVE-2026-48746: HTTP requests to a vLLM OpenAI-compatible endpoint where the Host header carries reserved URL characters (`/`, `?`) that the attacker injects to make starlette's `URL(scope=scope).path` resolve to a non-`/v1` path while FastAPI routing still serves the `/v1` API. Targets vLLM 0.3.0 ≤ v < 0.22.0 directly exposed (no RFC-conforming reverse proxy in front). Rationale: Article body explicitly names the bypass primitive: 'an attacker to include special URL characters such as `/` or `?` in the Host: header'. Any inbound request to `/v1/*` with `/` or `?` in the Host header is RFC-7230-non-compliant and points directly at CVE-2026-48746 exploitation; the GHSA advisory itself is the authoritative second source for the affected range (vllm 0.3.0 ≤ v < 0.22.0). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured upstream proxy that forwards a virtual-host string containing a path segment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus, Tenable, Qualys) running the CVE-2026-48746 plugin
  • Pen-test / red-team reproducing the PoC during an authorised engagement
  • Old IIS server bug where Host header is set to URL fragment by a legacy client (rare)
  • Custom internal tooling that uses host:port/path style proxying
Suppression filter
// suppress known scanners and internal pen-test source ranges
| where SrcIp !in ("<vuln_scanner_ip>", "<redteam_jumphost_ip>")
| where HostHdr !startswith "qualys" and HostHdr !startswith "nessus"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pivot on SrcIp — pull all /v1/* requests from that source in the last 24h, decode the Host header to see the injected path/query, check whether HTTP 200 responses followed (successful bypass) vs 4xx (blocked). 2. Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, take the vLLM instance off the internet (revoke NSG/SG public ingress) until you can place an RFC-conforming proxy (nginx, ALB) in front per the advisory's mitigation note. 3. Hunt: enumerate every vLLM deployment via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory where SoftwareName=='vllm' and SoftwareVersion < 0.22.0, audit which are internet-facing without a reverse proxy, review their access logs for the same Host-header pattern across the last 30 days, and check the model/prompt logs for unexpected inference calls that may indicate model-theft or data-exfil during the bypass window.
// vLLM CVE-2026-48746 — Host header carrying / or ? against a vLLM /v1/* endpoint
// Path 1: nginx/vllm access logs shipped via Syslog
let vllm_syslog =
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "/v1/"
    | extend HostHdr = extract(@'"Host:\s*([^"\r\n]+)"', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | extend ReqPath = extract(@'"(?:GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)\s+(/v1/[^\s"]+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | extend SrcIp   = extract(@'(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(ReqPath)
    | where HostHdr matches regex @"[/?]"      // RFC 7230 forbids these in Host header
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SrcIp, HostHdr, ReqPath, SyslogMessage;
// Path 2: CEF/WAF in front of vLLM
let vllm_cef =
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has "/v1/"
    | where DestinationHostName matches regex @"[/?]"
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceProduct;
union vllm_syslog, vllm_cef
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7d3a8c41-9f06-4a2b-b8a4-2e7d6f1a9c10
status: experimental
description: Detects HTTP requests against vLLM /v1/* endpoints where the Host header contains reserved URL characters ('/' or '?') used to bypass starlette AuthenticationMiddleware (CVE-2026-48746).

  condition: selection_path and selection_host_inject
falsepositives:
  - Misconfigured reverse proxy passing through SNI-style virtual host values
  - Internal pen testers validating the CVE

vLLM /v1/* API access without Authorization header on auth-configured instance AIExploitation Medium
Hunts requests to vLLM OpenAI-compatible API endpoints (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/models, /v1/embeddings) that arrive without an Authorization: Bearer header on a deployment that has VLLM_API_KEY / --api-key set. Successful 200 responses under these conditions are a direct symptom of CVE-2026-48746 exploitation or other middleware misconfiguration. Rationale: Article states the bypass 'allows to use the API without providing the configured VLLM_API_KEY or --api-key'. Endpoint set is the documented OpenAI-compatible surface vLLM exposes under /v1. A 200 with no Authorization Bearer on these paths is the post-bypass signature; correlates the reviewer-suggested credential-access pivot to the article's specific endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6 • https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/serving/openai_compatible_server.html
ATT&CKT1556 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • vLLM deployments intentionally running without API key (legitimate, no auth configured)
  • Health-check probes from Kubernetes liveness/readiness hitting /v1/models without auth
  • Internal monitoring tooling using IP allowlist instead of bearer auth
  • Load balancer health pings
  • Initial /v1/models discovery calls from approved client SDKs before they read the token from env
Suppression filter
| where SrcIp !in ("<k8s_node_cidr>", "<healthcheck_lb_ip>")
| where SyslogMessage !contains "kube-probe"
| where SyslogMessage !contains "ELB-HealthChecker"
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the target vLLM instance has VLLM_API_KEY or --api-key set (check systemd unit, docker-compose, or k8s manifest env) — if no API key is configured, this is by design, suppress and tag the host. 2. Contain: if API key IS configured, treat as confirmed bypass — block the source IP at edge, rotate VLLM_API_KEY, restart vLLM, and front the listener with nginx per advisory mitigation. 3. Hunt: pull all /v1/chat/completions and /v1/completions bodies from the suspect window — look for prompts that exfiltrate system prompts, leak training data via membership inference, or attempt prompt injection chains. Check egress for the same source pulling /v1/models repeatedly (recon).
// vLLM /v1/* requests lacking Authorization: Bearer that succeeded (200)
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/v1/chat/completions","/v1/completions","/v1/models","/v1/embeddings")
| extend ReqMethod = extract(@'"(GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)\s', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend ReqPath   = extract(@'"(?:GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)\s+(/v1/[^\s"]+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend Status    = toint(extract(@'"\s(\d{3})\s', 1, SyslogMessage))
| extend SrcIp     = extract(@'^(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend HasAuth   = SyslogMessage matches regex @'(?i)authorization:\s*Bearer\s+\S+'
| where isnotempty(ReqPath)
| where Status == 200
| where HasAuth == false
| summarize Requests=count(), Paths=make_set(ReqPath, 10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIp, Computer
| where Requests >= 1
| order by Requests desc

status: experimental
description: Detects HTTP requests against vLLM OpenAI-compatible /v1/* endpoints that lack an Authorization Bearer token, indicative of CVE-2026-48746 bypass when the deployment has VLLM_API_KEY configured.
references:

vLLM 401/403 followed by 200 on /v1/* from same source IP within short window AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the exploitation timeline of CVE-2026-48746: an attacker first probes vLLM auth (receiving 401/403 because they have no token), then within a short window obtains 200 responses on the same /v1/* endpoints from the same source IP without ever presenting valid credentials. Encodes the failure→success transition the reviewer flagged. Rationale: Reviewer suggestion 3, anchored to the article's auth-bypass narrative. A single source IP receiving 401/403 then 200 on /v1/* within 10 minutes — without a credential change — is exactly the exploit timeline the article describes (probe → bypass via Host header → unauthorised inference). Time-window correlation cuts the broad 'no Authorization header' baseline noise. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6
ATT&CKT1556 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User mistyped API key, fixed it, and continued (legitimate fix)
  • Client SDK rotating to a freshly-issued token mid-session
  • Health probe failing then a real authenticated client succeeding shortly after (NAT/proxy sharing source IP)
  • Intermittent reverse-proxy auth header stripping on retry
  • CI pipeline fetching a token from a vault between failure and retry
Suppression filter
| where SrcIp !in ("<corp_nat_gateway>", "<ci_runner_egress_ip>")
| extend FailHasToken = SyslogMessage matches regex @'(?i)authorization:\s*Bearer\s+\S+'
| where FailHasToken == false  // only the credential-less failure->success path
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the raw request lines for both the failing and succeeding calls from this SrcIp — compare the Authorization header values. If the failures had NO Authorization and the successes also had NO Authorization (or the same invalid one), this is the bypass; if the failures had an invalid token and successes had a valid one, it's a benign credential fix. 2. Contain: on confirmed bypass, block SrcIp at edge, rotate VLLM_API_KEY, and deploy nginx in front per advisory mitigation. 3. Hunt: enumerate every /v1/chat/completions body from SrcIp in the success window, look for prompts probing internal data or system-prompt extraction; check whether SrcIp also performed Host-header injection (correlate to UC1) — co-occurrence is high-confidence exploitation evidence.
// Auth failure -> success transition on vLLM /v1/* from the same source IP within 10 min
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
let vllm_reqs =
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "/v1/"
    | extend ReqPath = extract(@'"(?:GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)\s+(/v1/[^\s"]+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | extend Status  = toint(extract(@'"\s(\d{3})\s', 1, SyslogMessage))
    | extend SrcIp   = extract(@'^(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(ReqPath) and isnotempty(SrcIp);
let failures =
    vllm_reqs
    | where Status in (401, 403)
    | project FailTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIp, Computer, FailPath = ReqPath;
let successes =
    vllm_reqs
    | where Status in (200, 201)
    | project SuccTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIp, Computer, SuccPath = ReqPath;
failures
| join kind=inner successes on SrcIp, Computer
| where SuccTime between (FailTime .. FailTime + WindowMinutes)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', SuccTime, FailTime)
| summarize FailCount=count(), FirstFail=min(FailTime), FirstSuccess=min(SuccTime), Paths=make_set(SuccPath, 10) by SrcIp, Computer
| where FailCount >= 1
| order by FirstSuccess desc

Langflow CVE-2026-48519: POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp with embedded Python code AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated exploitation of Langflow's Shareable Playground RCE. The exploit POSTs to /api/v1/build_public_tmp/<flow-id>/flow with a JSON body whose data.nodes[].data.node.template.code.value field carries arbitrary Python — fires on the exact endpoint+payload pattern named in the advisory PoC. Rationale: Hardcoded to the literal endpoint path '/api/v1/build_public_tmp' named in the GHSA advisory body and PoC cURL. POST/PUT-only because the vulnerable code path requires a JSON body with the malicious nodes[].data.node.template.code.value field. Cross-checked with NVD entry for CVE-2026-48519 and the langflow-ai/langflow GitHub release notes for 1.9.1. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5ff-9q35-q26f • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48519 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user accessing a Shareable Playground link they were intentionally given
  • Langflow developer testing flows locally during development
  • Internal QA/load-testing tools exercising the endpoint
  • Browser auto-replays of saved POST requests from devtools session
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys) probing the path for CVE-2026-48519
Suppression filter
| where not (ClientIP in ("<known-admin-ip-1>","<known-admin-ip-2>") and UserAgent has_any ("Mozilla","Chrome","Firefox") and BytesIn < 2048)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full POST body for the matching request and check whether data.nodes[].data.node.template.code.value contains Python builtins (exec, eval, __import__, subprocess, os.system, socket) or shell tokens (touch, curl, wget, bash, /tmp/, /dev/shm). A benign Shareable Playground click sends only stock chat-input wiring. Step 2 (contain): If malicious payload confirmed, block the source IP at the edge, disable the affected public flow (DELETE on the flow's public_id), and isolate the Langflow host pending forensics. If patch is available, upgrade to >1.9.1 immediately. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the Langflow host's outbound network for the next 24h for any new domains/IPs, check /tmp /dev/shm and the Langflow working directory for new files, and grep langflow logs for other public flow IDs hit by the same client_id cookie or source IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp" or AdditionalFields has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let LangflowHits_IIS = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
    | where csMethod in~ ("POST","PUT")
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP = cIP, UriStem = csUriStem, UriQuery = csUriQuery, Method = csMethod, Status = scStatus, UserAgent = csUserAgent, BytesIn = csBytes;
let LangflowHits_CEF = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
    | where RequestMethod in~ ("POST","PUT")
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DestinationHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, UriStem = RequestURL, UriQuery = RequestContext, Method = RequestMethod, Status = tostring(EventOutcome), UserAgent = RequestClientApplication, BytesIn = ReceivedBytes;
union isfuzzy=true LangflowHits_IIS, LangflowHits_CEF
| extend SuspiciousPayloadSize = iff(BytesIn > 1024, true, false)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow exploit reconnaissance: clustered errors against /api/v1/build_public_tmp AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects burst of HTTP 4xx/5xx responses from the Langflow /api/v1/build_public_tmp endpoint by a single source IP — the failure signature of attackers iterating flow IDs or malformed JSON payloads before landing a working CVE-2026-48519 exploit. Tunable threshold; defaults to >=10 errors per source IP within 10 minutes. Rationale: Pre-RCE recon shape — attackers iterating flow IDs (404), JSON shape (400), or malformed payloads (500) against the literal endpoint path '/api/v1/build_public_tmp' the advisory names. Threshold of 10/10min separates scanner activity from a single user re-clicking a stale share link. Cross-checked NVD CVE-2026-48519 detail and the langflow repository's build_public_tmp route handler. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5ff-9q35-q26f • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48519
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner sweep (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) probing for CVE-2026-48519
  • User repeatedly clicking a Shareable Playground link after the underlying flow was deleted (404 loop)
  • Frontend SPA bug causing a request retry loop against the endpoint
  • WAF blocking legitimate requests and generating 403s in a burst
  • Health-check / monitoring tools probing the endpoint without a valid flow ID
Suppression filter
| where ClientIP !in ("<scanner-ip-1>","<scanner-ip-2>") and UserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","masscan","healthcheck")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Look up the source IP in threat intel (Shodan, AbuseIPDB, internal IOC list) and check what HTTP status codes dominate the burst — pure 404s suggest flow-ID guessing, mixed 400/500 suggests payload fuzzing, pure 403 suggests WAF blocking. Step 2 (contain): If external + non-scanner, block the source IP at the WAF/edge and rate-limit the /api/v1/build_public_tmp path globally. If internal, identify the scanner and exclude the IP from this rule. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the source IP for any successful (HTTP 200) calls to the same endpoint in the surrounding 30 minutes — those are the exploitation attempt that landed. Cross-reference with UC1 (POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp).

          by RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where HitCount >= 10
| order by Timestamp desc

let Threshold = 10;

union isfuzzy=true IIS_Errors, CEF_Errors

          by ClientIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowSize)

Langflow Python runtime spawning shell/subprocess children (post-exploit RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-48519: the Langflow Python worker (uvicorn/gunicorn/python running langflow) spawning sh/bash/cmd or invoking touch/curl/wget/socket-bind. The PoC payload literally runs 'touch /tmp/pwned' via the injected node code, so any non-trivial subprocess from the Langflow runtime is highly suspicious. Rationale: Article PoC literally executes 'touch /tmp/pwned' via the data.nodes[].data.node.template.code.value field — this UC catches that exact payload plus the broader family of shell/network/filesystem children that a Langflow worker has no business spawning. Stacktrace in the advisory confirms langflow runs in a Python interpreter (likely uvicorn/gunicorn), so parent-process filter on those binaries is high-fidelity. Cross-checked langflow Dockerfile in the langflow-ai/langflow repo for default entrypoint. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5ff-9q35-q26f • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48519
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow flow with a legitimate ShellTool / BashTool component that intentionally invokes shell commands
  • Container healthcheck script running curl/wget against localhost from inside the Langflow pod
  • Operator exec'ing into the Langflow container to run diagnostics (touch, ls, cat)
  • Langflow's own pip install / package management invoking sh during component installation
  • CI/CD pipeline running smoke tests that invoke Python -> shell from inside a Langflow image build
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("healthcheck","pip install","apt-get","yum install") and Account in~ ("root","langflow","app") and ParentImage has "entrypoint")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the child process command line and the parent's recent network activity. If the child is 'touch /tmp/pwned' or any literal from the advisory's PoC, treat as confirmed exploit. Otherwise check whether the command line matches a known Langflow ShellTool component used in this deployment. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the Langflow host/container, capture memory if feasible, suspend all public_flow IDs (set is_public=false in the DB), and rotate any credentials/API keys the Langflow runtime had access to (LLM API keys, vector DB creds, internal service tokens). Patch to langflow >1.9.1. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep DeviceFileEvents for new files written by the python parent in /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp, and the Langflow working directory in the last 7 days. Sweep outbound network from the Langflow host for new external IPs/domains. Pivot on UC1 (POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp) to identify the originating exploit request and source IP.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","python.exe","uvicorn","gunicorn")
      or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow","build_public_tmp")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","touch","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","chmod","base64")
      or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/pwned","touch /tmp/","touch /dev/shm","bash -i","sh -c","-c \"import os\"","socket.socket","subprocess.Popen","os.system")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspChildren = dynamic(["sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","touch","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","chmod","base64"]);
let SuspCmdTokens = dynamic(["/tmp/pwned","touch /tmp/","touch /dev/shm","bash -i","sh -c","subprocess.Popen","os.system","socket.socket"]);
let WinHits = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn") or CommandLine has "langflow"
    | where tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]) in~ (SuspChildren) or CommandLine has_any (SuspCmdTokens)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, ParentImage = ParentProcessName, ChildImage = NewProcessName, ChildCmd = CommandLine;
let AsimHits = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn") or ParentProcessCommandLine has "langflow"
    | where TargetProcessName has_any (SuspChildren) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (SuspCmdTokens)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, ParentImage = ParentProcessName, ChildImage = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine;
union isfuzzy=true WinHits, AsimHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NTFS junction creation via cmd.exe mklink /J AIInstallation High
Detects the foundational primitive of the GhostTree EDR-evasion technique: a user-mode process invoking cmd.exe with `mklink /J` to create an NTFS directory junction. The article confirms only write permissions are needed (no admin) and that the same syntax is used to build the recursive Parent\Child loop. Rationale: Anchors on the exact two-token combination from Code Block 1 (`mklink /J`) inside cmd.exe — the verbatim invocation the article gives as the GhostBranch/GhostTree primitive. Legit non-admin junction creation is rare outside of WSL/dev setup, making this a high-fidelity signal even before correlating multiple events.
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WSL/Docker Desktop install routines creating junctions under %LOCALAPPDATA%
  • Veeam, Acronis or other backup tooling staging shadow-copy mount points via mklink
  • Developer scripts symlinking node_modules or build output between projects
  • Group Policy folder-redirection scripts setting up profile junctions
  • Windows In-place upgrade / setup leaving mklink invocations in setupact context
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("wsl.exe", "docker.exe", "setup.exe", "msiexec.exe", "veeam.backup.shell.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\System32\" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("services.exe", "trustedinstaller.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full junction target path from CommandLine and inspect with `fsutil reparsepoint query <path>` and `dir /AL <parent>` — confirm whether the link target points to its own parent or ancestor (the GhostTree shape). Check parent process: if it's explorer.exe / a shell launched from a user-clicked .lnk or unsigned .bat, treat as malicious. Step 2 (contain): On the affected host, enumerate the junction target with `fsutil reparsepoint delete <path>` to break the loop, then run a Defender full scan of the previously-unscannable parent folder. Isolate host if any binaries are dropped alongside the junction. Step 3 (hunt): Across the fleet, search DeviceFileEvents for executable writes into the same parent folder within +/- 60 minutes of the junction creation, and pivot on the AccountName for other anomalous cmd.exe invocations in the last 7 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "mklink" and ProcessCommandLine has "/J"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe"
| where CommandLine has "mklink" and CommandLine has "/J"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NTFS reparse point manipulation via fsutil reparsepoint AIInstallation High
Detects the alternate API used to create or modify NTFS reparse points: `fsutil.exe reparsepoint`. GhostTree only needs a junction-style reparse point, and fsutil is the LOLBin path an attacker uses when mklink is blocked or audited. Pairs with the mklink detection to close the obvious bypass. Rationale: fsutil reparsepoint is the documented Windows API for the exact same NTFS reparse-point primitive the article describes. Attackers blocked from cmd's mklink will pivot here. Selecting on the `create`/`set` subcommands filters out the noisier read-only `query` usage that sysadmins run for troubleshooting.
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Storage admin running fsutil reparsepoint to repair a broken mount point
  • Backup software setting reparse points for VSS / dedup tags
  • Windows servicing stack (DISM / TrustedInstaller) tagging WinSxS folders
  • Container runtime tooling configuring layer mount reparse points
  • IT scripts converting roaming-profile junctions during migrations
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("trustedinstaller.exe", "dism.exe", "setup.exe", "veeam.backup.shell.exe", "dedupproc.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel != "System" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("services.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the full CommandLine and the target path; query the resulting reparse point with `fsutil reparsepoint query <path>` to determine reparse tag (0xA0000003 = mount point/junction) and the substitute path. If the substitute path resolves to the parent or an ancestor of the link itself, treat as confirmed GhostTree. Step 2 (contain): Delete the reparse attribute with `fsutil reparsepoint delete <path>`, then immediately scan the containing folder with Defender / EDR full file scan. Preserve a forensic copy of any executables that emerge from the previously-unscannable directory. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the AccountName and SubjectLogonId to find every fsutil and cmd.exe invocation in the last 30 days; specifically look for chained fsutil+mklink calls and for executable drops (DeviceFileEvents FileCreated where FolderPath = junction parent) within the same logon session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "fsutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "reparsepoint"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("create", "set")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\fsutil.exe"
| where CommandLine has "reparsepoint"
| where CommandLine has_any ("create", "set")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GhostTree pattern: multiple NTFS junctions created under same parent within minutes AIInstallation High
Detects the GhostTree giveaway: a single user/host issuing 2+ `mklink /J` commands inside a short window, which is the signature of building the binary-tree of `Child1`/`Child2` (or `P`/`B`) junctions the article describes. A single junction is benign; a burst of them under one user session is the recursive loop being constructed. Rationale: GhostBranch only needs one junction; GhostTree explicitly requires multiple (the article's Child1+Child2, or P+B examples). A 10-minute bucket with >=2 mklink /J invocations from the same user/host is the cleanest temporal signature of the technique being staged rather than a one-off legitimate junction. The bin/summarize structure stays inside canonical DeviceProcessEvents columns (DeviceName, AccountName, Timestamp) — no extracted-path columns required.
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WSL or Docker install creating multiple junctions during first-run setup
  • Developer batch script setting up multiple symlinked module directories in one go
  • Migration tool batch-creating junctions for legacy app path compatibility
  • Backup product staging multiple VSS mount-point junctions during snapshot prep
  • Group Policy logon script redirecting several profile folders via junction
Suppression filter
| where ParentProc !in~ ("wsl.exe", "docker.exe", "setup.exe", "msiexec.exe", "veeam.backup.shell.exe", "dism.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each junction created in the burst, run `fsutil reparsepoint query <path>` and `dir /AL <parent>` to map the link graph. If any junction's substitute path resolves to its own parent or ancestor, the recursive loop is confirmed and the containing folder is unscannable. Step 2 (contain): Delete each junction in the cluster with `fsutil reparsepoint delete <path>` (or `rmdir` — do NOT use `rd /s` which can follow the loop). Then isolate the host and trigger a full EDR scan of the now-flat parent directory. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the SubjectLogonId of the burst — pull every DeviceFileEvents FileCreated under that AccountName in +/- 4 hours, focusing on .exe/.dll/.ps1 writes that landed in the freed parent folder. Cross-check DeviceProcessEvents for any executable launched FROM that parent path post-junction-creation (the payload that was being hidden).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "mklink" and ProcessCommandLine has "/J"
| summarize JunctionCount = count(),
            SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine),
            ParentProc = any(InitiatingProcessFileName),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where JunctionCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe"
| where CommandLine has "mklink" and CommandLine has "/J"
| summarize JunctionCount = count(),
            SampleCmd = any(CommandLine),
            ParentProc = any(ParentProcessName),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by Computer, SubjectUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where JunctionCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\Cmd.exe) @CommandLine:(*mklink* OR *MKLINK*) @CommandLine:(*"/J"* OR *"/j"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\cmd\.exe$/i
| regex("mklink", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| regex("/J\\b", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| bucket(span=10m, field=@timestamp)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, _bucket], function=count(as=JunctionCount))
| JunctionCount >= 2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as JunctionCount, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Processes.process) as SampleCmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" Processes.process="*mklink*" Processes.process="* /J *" by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where JunctionCount >= 2 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count as JunctionCount, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Processes.process) as SampleCmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" Processes.process="*mklink*" Processes.process="* /J *" by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where JunctionCount >= 2 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime

New Rokarolla Android Malware Steals PINs, SMS Codes, and Crypto Wallet Funds

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 5 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Security researchers at&nbsp;Zimperium's zLabs&nbsp;have documented a new Android banking trojan, Rokarolla, that targets 217 banking and cryptocurrency apps and packs 137 remote commands. Together, they give an operator near-total control of an infected phone: it lifts lock-screen PINs, reads and sends SMS, rewrites the clipboard to redirect crypto payments, and switches off Google Play

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1555.003
Domainsberalisvc.info

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Rokarolla Android banking trojan C2 contact — beralisvc.info · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Rokarolla Android banking trojan C2 contact — beralisvc.info AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS resolution or HTTP(S) network traffic to beralisvc.info, the named command-and-control domain for the Rokarolla Android banking trojan documented by Zimperium zLabs in June 2026. The malware is named after this C2 family; any successful resolution from a managed mobile device, BYOD on corporate Wi-Fi, or corporate egress path is a near-certain indicator of an infected Android device performing overlay-credential exfiltration, SMS OTP theft, or accessibility-driven screenshot upload. Rationale: Anchored on the single hard IOC the article names — the C2 domain beralisvc.info — which the malware family is itself named after (Zimperium named it after the C2 servers). Behavioral TTPs in the article (Accessibility abuse, default-SMS-app hijack, overlay credential theft, screenshot-via-Accessibility exfiltration) require mobile-EDR-specific telemetry that isn't part of the standard Defender/Sentinel/Falcon/Datadog schemas in this prompt, so additional UCs would either restate this network IOC or hallucinate column names. One sharp detection beats five generic mobile templates. Cross-checked against The Hacker News, Infosecurity Magazine, and HackRead — all three independent write-ups attribute the campaign to Zimperium zLabs and confirm the C2-naming convention. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-rokarolla-android-malware-steals.html • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/rokarolla-android-banking-trojan/ • https://hackread.com/rokarolla-android-trojan-crypto-and-banking-apps/ • https://zimperium.com/blog/android-bankers-4-campaigns-in-a-row
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1437.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analysis sandbox / detonation VM resolving the IOC after a sample upload
  • Threat intel platform (MISP, OpenCTI, ThreatConnect) running automated enrichment lookups against the published IOC
  • Browser link-unfurling or preview services automatically fetching domain context when SOC analysts share the article in chat
  • SOC engineer manually pinging or curl-checking the domain during this very investigation
  • Mobile DFIR lab triaging a captured device with live C2 still active
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("malware-sandbox-01","ti-detonation-vm","sandbox-android-01","misp-enrichment-host") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl.exe","curl","wget.exe","wget","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe","python3") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "misp" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "opencti"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceInfo (OSPlatform, JoinType, LoggedOnUsers) for the resolving device. If Android, identify owner via MDM/Intune and confirm BYOD vs corporate-owned. If Windows/Linux or a known analyst workstation, validate against TI-sandbox/IR-tooling allowlist before escalating. Capture the InitiatingProcessFileName — on Android Defender this surfaces the offending package name. 2) Contain: for confirmed end-user mobile infections, issue Intune retire-and-wipe (factory reset is required; reinstall-only leaves the dropper). Force credential rotation for every banking, crypto-exchange, wallet, email, and SSO account ever used on the device. Sinkhole beralisvc.info and *.beralisvc.info at the corporate resolver and egress firewall. Notify the user's bank fraud team — SMS-OTP capture means recent transactions may be attacker-initiated. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for the prior 14 days for other newly-resolved low-reputation .info/.top/.xyz domains (fallback C2), elevated counts of 
let C2Domains = dynamic(["beralisvc.info"]);
let Lookback = 14d;
union isfuzzy=true
( DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
       or RemoteUrl endswith ".beralisvc.info"
  | extend Source = "DeviceNetworkEvents", QueryOrUrl = RemoteUrl
  | project Timestamp, Source, DeviceName, DeviceId, QueryOrUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName ),
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
       or RemoteUrl endswith ".beralisvc.info"
  | extend Source = "DeviceEvents/DnsQueryResponse", QueryOrUrl = RemoteUrl
  | project Timestamp, Source, DeviceName, DeviceId, QueryOrUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort = toint(0),
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName = AccountName )
| join kind=leftouter ( DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, JoinType, LoggedOnUsers) by DeviceId ) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, Source, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, JoinType, LoggedOnUsers,
          QueryOrUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domains = dynamic(["beralisvc.info"]);
let Lookback = 14d;
union isfuzzy=true
( DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
  | where Name has_any (C2Domains) or Name endswith ".beralisvc.info"
  | extend Source = "DnsEvents", QueryName = Name, ClientHost = Computer, Client = ClientIP
  | project TimeGenerated, Source, ClientHost, Client, QueryName, QueryType ),
( ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (C2Domains) or DnsQuery endswith ".beralisvc.info"
  | extend Source = "ImDnsActivity", QueryName = DnsQuery, ClientHost = DvcHostname, Client = SrcIpAddr, QueryType = DnsQueryTypeName
  | project TimeGenerated, Source, ClientHost, Client, QueryName, QueryType ),
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
  | where DestinationHostName has_any (C2Domains)
       or DestinationHostName endswith ".beralisvc.info"
       or RequestURL has "beralisvc.info"
  | extend Source = "CommonSecurityLog", QueryName = coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), ClientHost = SourceHostName, Client = SourceIP, QueryType = tostring(DestinationPort)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source, ClientHost, Client, QueryName, QueryType )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Rokarolla Android Banking Trojan C2 Domain Resolution (beralisvc.info)
id: 9b3c6f5d-1e7a-4b2c-8d9f-5a3e1c8b7d2f
description: Detects DNS resolution requests for beralisvc.info, the named command-and-control domain of the Rokarolla Android banking trojan reported by Zimperium zLabs in June 2026. The malware family is named after this C2 cluster and any resolution from a managed device strongly indicates an infected Android endpoint.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-rokarolla-android-malware-steals.html
    - https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/rokarolla-android-banking-trojan/
    - https://hackread.com/rokarolla-android-trojan-crypto-and-banking-apps/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
    - attack.t1071.001
    - attack.t1071.004
    - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
    category: dns
detection:
    selection_exact:
        query: 'beralisvc.info'
    selection_sub:
        query|endswith: '.beralisvc.info'
    condition: selection_exact or selection_sub
falsepositives:
    - Malware analysis sandbox detonating the sample
    - Threat intel enrichment tooling pre-resolving published IOCs
level: high
(@dns.question.name:(*beralisvc.info OR *.beralisvc.info OR *BERALISVC.INFO) OR @network.destination.domain:(*beralisvc.info OR *BERALISVC.INFO) OR @http.url:*beralisvc.info OR @url.domain:*beralisvc.info) AND -source:vulnerability_management
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)beralisvc\.info$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=[count(as=Hits), min(@timestamp, as=FirstSeen), max(@timestamp, as=LastSeen)])
| sort(FirstSeen, order=asc)

    | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

]

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Pickle in the Middle – Hijacking Vertex AI Model Uploads for Cross-Tenant RCE

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-06-16 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK install (CVE-2026-2473 — pre-1.148.0)
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Vertex AI default staging bucket squatting — predictable bucket pattern access · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Pickle in the Middle – Hijacking Vertex AI Model Uploads for Cross-Tenant RCE

Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK install (CVE-2026-2473 — pre-1.148.0) AIWeaponization High
Detects installation or invocation of google-cloud-aiplatform Python SDK at versions 1.139.0 through 1.147.x, which silently fall back to an attacker-owned GCS bucket via the deterministic `<project>-vertex-staging-<location>` pattern when no explicit staging bucket is supplied. Catches both first-time installs and runtime use of vulnerable libraries that should be upgraded to ≥1.148.0. Rationale: Pins to the EXACT vulnerable SDK version range disclosed in the Unit 42 article (1.139.0 — 1.147.x; fixed in 1.148.0 released 2026-04-15). The version regex eliminates noise from already-patched installs. Catches both interactive pip installs and CI/CD pipelines pulling pinned vulnerable versions. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://pypi.org/project/google-cloud-aiplatform/#history
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data science teams legitimately running pinned but outdated SDK versions in research notebooks
  • CI/CD pipelines re-installing an old pinned version in lockfiles awaiting upgrade
  • Docker image rebuilds replaying historical pip install commands from cached layers
  • Developers reproducing a known issue against a specific old SDK version for support tickets
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("docker.exe","buildkitd.exe") and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","download","--no-deps"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user and pull the full pip-install context — is this a developer workstation, build agent, or production ML pipeline? Check whether the SDK is actively used (search for `aiplatform.Model.upload` calls in the same project). 2) Contain: force-upgrade google-cloud-aiplatform to ≥1.148.0 in the affected environment; if the host has uploaded models in the last 7 days, treat any default-named staging buckets as suspect and verify ownership via `gcloud storage buckets describe`. 3) Hunt: pivot to GCS audit logs for any bucket matching `<project-id>-vertex-staging-<location>` and confirm the bucket resides in the customer's own project, not an attacker-controlled one. Check Vertex AI Model Registry for models uploaded during the vulnerable window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pip","pip3","python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"google-cloud-aiplatform==1\.(139|140|141|142|143|144|145|146|147)\."
| extend VulnerableVersion = extract(@"google-cloud-aiplatform==(1\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountUpn, VulnerableVersion, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "pip.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "pip3.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "python3.exe"
| where CommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"google-cloud-aiplatform==1\.(139|140|141|142|143|144|145|146|147)\."
| extend VulnerableVersion = extract(@"google-cloud-aiplatform==(1\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, CommandLine)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, SubjectUserName, VulnerableVersion, CommandLine, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vertex AI default staging bucket squatting — predictable bucket pattern access AIDelivery Medium
Hunts GCP audit logs for storage operations on buckets matching the deterministic `<project-id>-vertex-staging-<location>` pattern where the acting identity is NOT the customer's Vertex AI P4SA (`service-<project-num>@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com`) or a known internal pipeline service account. Surfaces both cross-tenant bucket squatting and unexpected writes that could be model-artifact poisoning. Rationale: Targets the exact bucket-name pattern from the article (`staging_bucket_name = project + "-vertex-staging-" + location`). Filtering OUT the legitimate Vertex AI P4SA isolates the access path the attacker would use — either bucket-squatting from a different project or an unexpected internal principal touching the staging bucket. Sigma omitted because this requires aggregation/exclusion logic not expressible as single-event-shape. Falcon/Defender/CloudWatch empty because this is GCP-native telemetry with no Falcon FDR or Microsoft endpoint equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-agents
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1525 T1530
Data sourcesWeb Change
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Customer DevOps service account legitimately reading the staging bucket during pipeline orchestration
  • Terraform/IaC service account creating or auditing the bucket during infra provisioning
  • Cloud Storage Transfer Service or Backup service principals enumerating buckets
  • Internal user using `gcloud storage` CLI for ad-hoc model artifact inspection
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm bucket ownership with `gcloud storage buckets describe gs://<bucket>` — if the project_number doesn't match your project, you've been squatted; treat as confirmed. Inventory any model artifacts already staged there. 2) Contain: immediately delete and recreate the bucket explicitly under your project, then upgrade the SDK to ≥1.148.0 across all clients. Revoke any models uploaded during the vulnerable window from the Vertex AI Model Registry and redeploy from a verified source. 3) Hunt: pull Vertex AI deployment events for the affected region and inspect model artifacts (`gsutil cat gs://<bucket>/.../model.joblib | python -c 'import pickletools; pickletools.dis(...)'`) for `__reduce__` payloads. Check IAM audit logs for any new permissions granted to external principals.
GCPAuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ServiceName == "storage.googleapis.com"
| extend BucketName = extract(@"projects/_/buckets/([^/]+)", 1, tostring(ResourceName))
| where BucketName matches regex @"-vertex-staging-(us|europe|asia|australia|northamerica|southamerica)"
| extend Principal = tostring(AuthenticationInfo.principalEmail)
| where Principal !endswith "@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Methods=make_set(MethodName), Principals=make_set(Principal), EventCount=count() by BucketName
| order by LastSeen desc
source:gcp.audit @protoPayload.serviceName:storage.googleapis.com @protoPayload.resourceName:*-vertex-staging-* -@protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail:*@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)

SecurityEvent

China-Linked SprySOCKS Backdoor Expands to Windows with Driver-Based Stealth

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 7 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged two previously undocumented Windows variants of what was believed to be a Linux-only backdoor called SprySOCKS. "The Windows variants discovered are internally marked as WIN_DRV and WIN_PLUS," ESET said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "Both come with a hard-coded C&amp;C [command-and-control] configuration and support communication over TCP, UDP,

Print Spooler (spoolsv.exe) spawning svchost.exe child — SprySOCKS WIN_PLUS print-processor loader AIInstallation High
Hunts the WIN_PLUS execution chain where the Windows Print Spooler service is abused to load a first-stage loader as a print processor, which then injects the SprySOCKS loader into a newly spawned svchost.exe. spoolsv.exe spawning svchost.exe is not legitimate Windows behaviour and is the WIN_PLUS-specific pivot called out in the ESET write-up. Rationale: spoolsv.exe is never the legitimate parent of svchost.exe — svchost is started by services.exe with -k <svcgroup>. ESET's WIN_PLUS chain explicitly stages the SprySOCKS loader into a freshly created svchost child of spoolsv via a malicious print processor, making this parent/child pair article-specific and very low-FP. Cross-checked T1547.012 Print Processors technique mapping on MITRE ATT&CK. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/012/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/012/
ATT&CKT1547.012 T1055.012
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party print driver bundles (HP / Konica / Lexmark) that occasionally spawn helper svchost-like processes during driver install
  • Print spooler crash + WER svchost handoff during fault recovery on legacy hardware
  • Custom EDR/AV print monitoring helpers using svchost.exe as an invocation stub
  • Patch test labs running the spooler under a service-host harness
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\system32\\" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"-k\s+\w+")
Response runbook
Triage: pull the svchost child's process tree and command line plus the print processor DLL loaded by spoolsv in the 60s preceding the spawn (DeviceImageLoadEvents on the same DeviceId). Hash-check the loaded DLL and verify Authenticode — a SprySOCKS print processor will be unsigned or signed by an unknown CA. Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response, kill the spoolsv-spawned svchost, and remove the malicious print processor value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Environments\Windows x64\Print Processors. Hunt: pivot on the loader DLL hash across the org, look for kernel-driver service registrations matching UC2, and review egress for TCP/UDP/WebSocket callbacks from the injected svchost.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "spoolsv.exe"
| where FileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine !contains "-k "
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\spoolsv.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\svchost.exe"
| where CommandLine !contains "-k "
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, NewProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kernel driver service registered with .dat image path (SprySOCKS DriverLoader pattern) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a Windows kernel-mode driver service whose ImagePath references a .dat file — matching the SprySOCKS WIN_DRV pattern where the encrypted DriverLoader (KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat) loads the RawWNPF rootkit driver (KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat). Legitimate kernel drivers ship as .sys, so a kernel service with a .dat image is highly anomalous. Rationale: Legitimate kernel-mode drivers ship as .sys; an ImagePath ending in .dat combined with ServiceType kernel/filesystem is highly anomalous. ESET disclosed the exact filenames (KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat DriverLoader, KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat RawWNPF) so the regex anchors on the SprySOCKS naming pattern while still catching naming-scheme variants. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1014/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1014
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vendor utilities that ship encrypted blobs renamed .dat and load them via a kernel driver (rare; some EDR/sandbox vendors)
  • Legacy backup or VPN clients that historically registered a kernel-mode helper with a .dat config path
  • Custom in-house driver development on engineering workstations using non-standard extensions
  • Anti-cheat or DRM drivers using .dat container files for the kernel image
Suppression filter
and not ServiceFileName has_any ("\\program files\\", "\\program files (x86)\\")
Response runbook
Triage: pull the ServiceFileName from disk, capture SHA256 plus Authenticode signing details and check whether the file lives outside %SystemRoot%\System32\drivers — an unsigned .dat in a writable directory is a near-certain rootkit. Contain: stop and delete the service via Defender Live Response, quarantine the .dat file, and snapshot memory for the loaded driver before reboot to preserve kernel state. Hunt: pivot org-wide on the filename pattern KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat / KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat and on the resulting SHA256; look for scheduled tasks dropped in the prior 24h and for the WIN_PLUS spoolsv→svchost chain in UC1 on adjacent hosts.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
| extend Extra = parse_json(AdditionalFields)
| extend ImagePath = tostring(Extra.ServiceFileName)
| extend SvcType = tostring(Extra.ServiceType)
| where ImagePath endswith ".dat"
   or ImagePath matches regex @"K[WX]1B5206BDC1743[A-Z0-9]{2}\.dat"
| where SvcType has_any ("KernelModeDriver", "FileSystemDriver", "1", "2") or isempty(SvcType)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ImagePath, SvcType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceType has_any ("kernel mode driver", "file system driver", "0x1", "0x2")
| where ServiceFileName has ".dat"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SprySOCKS WIN_DRV component .dat filenames written to disk (RawWNPF / DriverLoader) AIInstallation High
Hunts file-write events for the hard-coded SprySOCKS WIN_DRV driver-component filenames disclosed by ESET — KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat (RawWNPF rootkit driver) and KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat (encrypted DriverLoader). Any match is a high-confidence indicator of WIN_DRV deployment. Rationale: Filenames are hard-coded SprySOCKS WIN_DRV components disclosed in ESET's report. No legitimate software ships files matching the K[WX]1B5206BDC1743**.dat pattern; the regex anchors catch sibling variants under the same naming convention. Any hit is investigate-immediately. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1014/
ATT&CKT1014 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-research sandbox detonation environments storing malware samples with original filenames preserved
  • Forensic image acquisition tooling unpacking IR evidence on a managed endpoint
  • Security analyst downloading the ESET IOC bundle to their workstation
  • Honeypot or deception VMs intentionally seeded with these filenames for canary alerting
Suppression filter
and not FolderPath has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\malware-samples\\", "\\ir-evidence\\", "\\quarantine\\")
Response runbook
Triage: capture SHA256 of the dropped file and the InitiatingProcess that wrote it; cross-check against VirusTotal and ESET — a confirmed hash match is a critical incident requiring no further triage. Contain: isolate the host, kill the writing process tree, quarantine the file, and capture memory before reboot to preserve the kernel-driver state for forensics. Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 of the loader across the org, look for the scheduled task that triggered the DLL side-loading chain in the prior 24h, hunt for the kernel-driver service registration (UC2) and the spoolsv→svchost chain (UC1), and review egress for TCP/UDP/WebSocket callbacks from svchost/spoolsv lineage.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where FileName in~ ("KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat", "KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat")
   or FileName matches regex @"^K[WX]1B5206BDC1743[A-Z0-9]{2}\.dat$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat", "KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp

| order by conn_count desc

| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

description: |

    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.

Dozens of malicious wallpapers found on Steam Workshop: gamers’ accounts at risk

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-06-16 16 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Since late 2025, malware has been spreading rapidly through the Steam Workshop, the gaming platform's built-in service for players to create and share custom content. The attackers are primarily targeting gamers in China and Russia.

ATT&CKT1204.002 T1486 T1555.003
